title: Thymus Anatomy
descriptor: Mediastinal Position, Lobes & Structure, T Cell Maturation, Ageing, Thymus Disorders
intro: The thymus is a small lymphoid organ in the upper chest, lying behind the breastbone in the mediastinum. It has two lobes and, before birth and in childhood, helps the body make T lymphocytes, a type of white blood cell that helps protect against infection. At puberty the thymus begins to shrink and is gradually replaced by fat, so it is usually small by adulthood.

sections.heading: Location and relations
sections.body: The thymus lies in the superior part of the mediastinum, behind the sternum. The mediastinum is the part of the chest that lies between the sternum and the spinal column and between the lungs. The thymus is a bilobed organ, and its two lobes converge near the level of the manubrium of the sternum. Extensions of the thymus can rise into the neck towards the thyroid, and the number, size and position of the lobes vary a good deal between people. The two lobes form separately early in gestation and then migrate to fuse.

sections.heading: Structure and blood supply
sections.body:
Each lobe is divided into lobules, and each lobule has an outer cortex and an inner medulla. Immature T cells, called thymocytes, leave the bone marrow and mature largely in the thymus. The medulla is made up mainly of medullary thymic epithelial cells and dendritic cells. It contains concentric, whorled structures called Hassall's corpuscles, which are formed from epithelial cells.

The arterial supply of the thymus is variable. The main sources are the inferior thyroid artery and branches of the internal thoracic arteries, with smaller contributions from the pericardiophrenic and intercostal arteries. Venous drainage follows the arteries, and a large posterior vein drains into the left innominate (brachiocephalic) vein. The blood supply, lymphatic drainage and innervation of each lobe remain separate throughout life, even after the lobes have fused.

sections.heading: Function: training T cells
sections.body: The thymus is a primary lymphoid organ in which T lymphocytes proliferate and mature. Thymocytes are screened for tolerance there: cells that react with the body's own antigens are removed by negative selection, and only a small minority of thymocytes leave the thymus as mature, functional T cells. The autoimmune regulator (AIRE) protein, which works mainly in the thymus, helps eliminate T cells that could otherwise attack the body's own tissues. The mature T cells include helper, regulatory and cytotoxic types, which go on to take part in adaptive immune responses elsewhere, for example in lymph nodes.

sections.heading: Change with age and imaging
sections.body: The thymus is active and growing in childhood, when it makes white blood cells that fight infection. At puberty it starts to get smaller and is replaced by fat, and it is usually small by adulthood. This shrinkage, called involution, is thought to result from rising androgen levels in the circulation during puberty. On CT scans of adults, the appearance of the thymus changes with age as it is replaced by fat. In people with myasthenia gravis, described below, a chest CT scan is commonly used to check the thymus.

sections.heading: Clinical relevance: myasthenia gravis
sections.body: Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune condition in which antibodies interfere with the signal from nerves to muscles, causing weakness that worsens with activity and improves with rest. Eye symptoms such as drooping eyelids and double vision are often the first to appear, and other muscles can be affected, causing problems with swallowing, speech or breathing. Symptoms can be made worse by fatigue, overuse of a muscle, hot weather, infections or stress. Surgery to remove the thymus (thymectomy) can reduce the symptoms of myasthenia gravis, possibly by rebalancing the immune system.

sections.heading: Clinical relevance: tumours and underdevelopment
sections.body:
Cancer of the thymus, including thymoma and thymic carcinoma, is rare. Surgery to remove the tumour is the most common treatment, and radiation therapy, chemotherapy, chemoradiation and hormone therapy are other options. Treatment of an early-stage (stage I) thymoma is surgery.

Some people are born with an underdeveloped thymus. In 22q11.2 deletion syndrome, also called DiGeorge syndrome, the thymus can be underdeveloped (hypoplastic), which can lower the number of T cells in the blood. The effect on immunity depends mainly on whether the thymus is hypoplastic, severely hypoplastic or absent (aplastic).
